content.text: An array is a fundamental data structure in Java that allows you to store multiple elements of the same type in a contiguous block of memory. Arrays provide fast, index-based access to their elements and are widely used for their simplicity and efficiency.

items: Fixed Size: Arrays are created with a predefined size and cannot grow or shrink dynamically.
Homogeneous Data: All elements in an array must be of the same type.
Zero-Based Indexing: Array indexing starts at 0, with the first element at index 0 and the last element at length - 1.
Direct Access: Array elements can be accessed in constant time using their index.
Memory Efficiency: Arrays are stored in contiguous memory locations, leading to efficient access patterns.
Declaration: Use square brackets [] after the type to declare an array.
Initialization:

content.text: Array elements can be accessed and modified using their index:

content.code:
int[] scores = {90, 80, 70};
System.out.println(scores[1]);  // Output: 80
scores[1] = 85;                 // Modify element
System.out.println(scores[1]);  // Output: 85

content.text: Java supports multidimensional arrays, such as 2D arrays, often used for representing grids or matrices.

items: Efficient Access: Direct indexing provides constant-time access to elements.
Memory Compactness: Elements are stored in contiguous memory locations.
Ease of Use: Arrays are simple and intuitive for basic data storage and manipulation.
Fixed Size: Arrays cannot grow or shrink dynamically, which can lead to wasted memory or the need for resizing.
Type Homogeneity: Only elements of the same type can be stored.
No Built-in Methods: Arrays lack utility methods like those provided by the Java Collections Framework.
